title: Intonarumori (noise intoners)
lede: Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti stand among their intonarumori, wooden boxes with large metal horns built to play the music of Russolo’s manifesto The Art of Noises.
summary: Box-shaped noise machines with flaring horns, built by Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti in Milan, photographed c. 1913.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Luigi Russolo and assistant Ugo Piatti in their Milan studio with Intonarumori, 1913

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 2301 × 1821 px; a 1280 × 1013 px rendering was inspected and stored). The file is a photograph of a printed reproduction of the period photograph, by an unknown photographer. Commons says it was first published with Russolo’s *The Art of Noises*. The instruments themselves are lost: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori) says most were destroyed in Paris during the Second World War.

styles.note: The Futurist programme of noise and machines made into objects: musical instruments designed as plain industrial boxes and horns. Partial fit: the visual grammar of type and lines of force is absent.

context: Russolo invented and built the intonarumori from about 1910 to 1930, in 27 varieties. A wheel touched a string attached to a drum; a handle changed the string’s tension and pitch; a horn amplified the sound. [Wikipedia: Intonarumori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori).
They were built to perform the music described in Russolo’s 1913 manifesto *The Art of Noises*, published as a book in 1916. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori).

The Commons description names the men as Russolo and his assistant Ugo Piatti in their Milan studio. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_and_assistant_Ugo_Piatti_in_their_Milan_studio_with_Intonarumori,_L%E2%80%99Arte_dei_rumori_(The_Art_of_Noises),_1913.jpg).
observed: About fifteen instruments are stacked across the room. Each is a plain dark rectangular box with a large flaring metal horn, aimed in different directions.
The horns are smooth cones with a bright rim; there is no ornament on the boxes, only small handles and fittings.
Two men in suits stand behind the instruments at the center.
A tall cabinet with pipes stands at right; the floor has a hexagonal tile pattern and a lamp hangs from the ceiling.
The print is sepia with a strong glare at upper left.
interpretation: The instruments look like machinery, not like orchestral instruments. The pile of horns pointing in many directions is itself an image of simultaneous noise.
The photograph has become an emblem of the movement’s aim to bring industrial sound into art.
borrow: Repeat one simple industrial form, such as a horn or cone, in many sizes and directions to suggest noise.
Show sound as direction: aim shapes outward from a cluster.

images.alt: Sepia photograph of a room filled with dark box-shaped instruments with large flaring metal horns pointing in different directions. Two men in suits stand behind them; a lamp hangs from the ceiling and the floor has hexagonal tiles.
images.caption: Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti with the intonarumori in their Milan studio, c. 1913, photographer unknown. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_and_assistant_Ugo_Piatti_in_their_Milan_studio_with_Intonarumori,_L%E2%80%99Arte_dei_rumori_(The_Art_of_Noises),_1913.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain and says the photograph was first published with Russolo’s *The Art of Noises* (manifesto 1913, book 1916). Publication before 1931 makes it public domain in the United States. In Italy, a simple photograph is protected for 20 years from production, and Russolo (died 1947) and Piatti (died 1953) died more than 70 years ago, so the instruments shown are also public domain.
